      <title>Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/28/egypt-lina-attalah-mada-masr-press-freedom-clampdown</link>
      <description><p>Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website</p><p>Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.</p><p>Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/28/egypt-lina-attalah-mada-masr-press-freedom-clampdown">Continue reading...</a></description>

</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/12709f3a-d37d-11f1-ae1b-811458fcf026/w:1024/p:16x9/291026-BUSINESS-DAILY.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/12709f3a-d37d-11f1-ae1b-811458fcf026/w:1024/p:16x9/291026-BUSINESS-DAILY.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">d8ac8e18-d37b-11f1-867b-d5a7f61cce42</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 10:54:59 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Bryan QUINN</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Kenya's female athletes make their mark as Youth Olympic Games approach</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261029-kenya-s-female-athletes-make-their-mark-as-youth-olympic-games-approach</link><description>
Senegal is preparing to host the Youth Olympic Games, which begin this weekend. FRANCE 24's Bastien Renouil reports from the ground.

Oliver Farry is pleased to welcome Alex Vines, Africa Program Director at the European Council on Foreign Relations. He takes us through Russia's African paradox involving diplomatic Influence, security dependence and the politics of multipolarity. For Vines, the participation of 48 African countries and 22 heads of state and government in the latest Russia-Africa summit illustrates the continuing appeal,  of Moscow as a diplomatic and strategic partner.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/b68a66e4-d37f-11f1-9402-47de50b3c1e4/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261029-081049-081833-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/b68a66e4-d37f-11f1-9402-47de50b3c1e4/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261029-081049-081833-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">bbf072a4-d37f-11f1-b1fa-a939b9b14960</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 10:43:25 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Somalia: Lower house of parliament passes bill on sexual violence</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261029-somalia-lower-house-of-parliament-passes-bill-on-sexual-violence</link><description>

FRANCE 24's Bastien Renouil met with Sofia Rajab in Nairobi. <![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Thu, 29 Oct 2026 10:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ SpaceX's Starfall capsule delivers cargo for US Air Force in landmark 'point to point' space mission ]]> The U.S. Air Force is opening up about the SpaceX Starfall cargo capsule it flew on a recent rideshare mission to orbit — and showing off what the capsule carried.

The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) completed a point-to-point rocket cargo delivery test using the secretive uncrewed reentry vehicle, confirming on social media its recovery of the package in the Pacific Ocean. "With support from SpaceX, the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown," the AFRL wrote in an X post on Oct. 26.

The Starfall capsule launched on a Falcon 9 rocket as a part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, which lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20. Starfall carried a number of AFRL-developed cargo pods designed to transport military equipment through space and back to Earth. The successful recovery of the pods marks a big step forward in the Air Force's effort to examine the viability of point-to-point (P2D) rocket cargo missions.

"This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force," said AFRL Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly in a press release on Oct. 20.

Photos included in the AFRL social media post show military personnel unpacking a recovered cargo pod for inspection. Each pod contained sensors to monitor temperature conditions through launch, reentry and splashdown, as well as to measure the shock and vibration forces exerted on its cargo.

For its first Starfall mission, AFRL packed its cargo pods with representative items like medical equipment, food ration packs and other military kit that might be helpful for surviving an emergency somewhere that's tough to reach via conventional transportation. To that end, AFRL said it also conducted a fit check of a UNI-PAC III life raft inside Starfall, which could potentially be included in future tests.

"Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment and survival gear, including a SATCOM-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment," AFRL said in its release.

SpaceX's disk-shaped Starfall capsule made a quiet debut on a Falcon 9 launch in June, and the company has remained relatively quiet about the vehicle to date. Most of what we do know comes from a Federal Aviation Administration environmental assessment published earlier this year.

The hockey-puck-looking vehicle measures approximately 10.2 feet (3.1 meters) across and can return up to 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms) of cargo from orbit, according to that report. And it sports a carbon fiber heat shield and compressed gas thrusters for attitude control during reentry, as well as a parachute system for precision landings.

AFRL will assess the data recovered from the Oct. 20 mission to contribute to its broader Rocket Cargo initiative, which the Air Force hopes can evolve to the transportation of tens of tons of cargo per launch. That would exceed Starfall's mass capacity, but Starfall isn't the only vehicle the military has considered for its Rocket Cargo program.

SpaceX's much larger Starship rocket, which is still under development, was a likely candidate for tests at Johnston Atoll, a remote Pacific bird sanctuary where the Air Force proposed building a pair of landing pads for cargo delivery tests. However, those plans were suspended in July 2025 amid environmental concerns, and the status of the search for an alternative site is unclear.

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket ]]>

On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3.

This wasn't Britain's first satellite, but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow.

The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket. Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

The mission lifted off from the Woomera Range Complex in Australia. While the launch was a success, the rocket's final stage bumped into the satellite after it separated, and the collision broke one of Prospero's four radio antennas. But the satellite still worked, and it remained operational until 1973.

Why it mattered

The launch of Prospero is etched in the history books of British spaceflight. To this date, it remains the first and last British satellite ever launched on a native rocket built in the United Kingdom.

The 66-kilogram satellite launched on a three-stage Black Arrow R-3 rocket and flew in an elliptical orbit that ranged between 522 km to 1,300 km above the Earth. The rocket itself was based on the smaller Black Knight research rocket and stood nearly 13 meters tall. While the launch was successful, the Black Arrow program, which had seen two failures and two successes, was ultimately canceled.

The Prospero satellite, meanwhile, operated in orbit for two years, with regular communications ending in 1973, though it was contacted at least once each year through 1996, according to the BBC.

The satellite remains in orbit today, its legacy such that at least one company - the Scotland-based space startup Skyrora, has announced plans to retrieve Prospero in orbit and deorbit in Earth's atmosphere.

That Skyrora plan, announced in 2021, would use the company's space tug to rendezvous with the defunct Prospero, latch onto it and pull it from space. The company aims to launch its Skyrora XL rocket out of a Saxavord Spaceport in Scotland.

"By recovering Prospero, we are not only coming together as a space nation and taking responsibility for what we have launched into orbit, but also confirming our commitment to the sustainable use of outer space," Volodymyr Levykin, Skyrora founder and CEO, said at the time.

]]> <![CDATA[ 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station' ]]> Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface.

We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth. One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

This underwater habitat was called "La Chalupa" when it was built in the 1970s. Its purpose was to allow divers to live and perform research as aquanauts — people who spend more than 24 hours underwater in a so-called state of saturation. Today, the Jules' Undersea Lab is located near Key Largo, in Florida. However, it was originally designed to be mobile — inside a barge 20 feet wide and 60 feet long (6 to 18 meters).

The aquanauts could choose an ideal site for their research expeditions underwater and then have the facility be submerged. They did that by flooding most of its inside space, turning it from a boat to a submarine. Once their work was done, they could remove the water and move "La Chalupa" to another location.

Unfortunately, the funding to keep this facility running ran out over time, and it was moved one last time to its current home. Since then, the now Jules' Undersea Lab served as the research station for tens of different aquanaut missions, including a NASA 30-day project and two missions that set world records for the longest time living underwater (73 and 100 days).

On the inside, the underwater station is made up of a galley with a kitchen and dining/work area. Next to it there is a basic toilet, shower and the "moon pool," which is the equivalent of a door to get inside the habitat. The final area is the bedroom with two bunk beds, which can be split in the middle to create two bedrooms and provide additional privacy. Three windows throughout the habitat provide its dwellers with a view of a mostly green outside world.

To start our SEA STAR simulated space mission, we waved goodbye to our Mission Control team on "Earth" and dove down to enter the Jules' Undersea Lab through the "moon pool" at 25 feet (7.6 m) underwater. After that, we did not return to the surface again until five days later. We lived and worked the whole time underwater, performing our space-related research and "spacewalks" (a.k.a. exploration dives in scuba gear).

We were able to survive all this time in such a challenging environment thanks to a number of important life support systems keeping us alive. The communications and umbilical support cables (providing air, fresh water and power) for the habitat were originally supplied by NASA. All the piping and fittings are inside the submerged barge, protected from the air-sea interface and from encrusting marine creatures. There was also a direct line to Mission Control "on Earth" to help us in case of any emergencies.

Our schedule kept us busy all day every day to simulate what astronauts experience on the International Space Station (ISS). All four of us on the SEA STAR crew had research projects that we were responsible for, as well as daily tasks. ]]> <![CDATA[ ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live ]]>

The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years.

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

iROSAs lie on top of the existing, decades-old arrays on ISS, which are naturally degrading with age. The first iROSA rolled out in 2021. Once all eight are installed and running, the station will see its power supply rise from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts — a boost of roughly 30%.

A Canadian capcom, too

The capcom (capsule communicator) for both spacewalks will be CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons. She has experience in this role already, serving as a capcom on NASA's Artemis II mission around the moon this past April. And she'll serve as lead capcom for Artemis III, which will test crewed lunar landers in Earth orbit next summer, if all goes to plan.

Also helping Kutryk and Menon will be Canadian space technology, specifically Canadarm2 — the ISS robotic arm tasked for spacewalk support, among other maintenance duties.

"It's been busy preparing for the upcoming spacewalks," Menon said about Canadarm2 in a Saturday (Oct. 24) X post. Ground controllers recently moved the arm over to the "trunk" or storage area of a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft, which brought the two iROSA arrays up earlier this month.Canadarm2 picked up the IROSAs and moved them to a transporter for the astronauts. "It even loosened bolts for us before the spacewalks … I'm grateful for the help," Menon added.

During the Oct. 29 spacewalk, Canadarm2 will do even more. Kutryk and Menon will slide an array off its transport rail and then have Menon get onto a Canadarm2 platform, to put the array into his hands. From inside the ISS, NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins will carefully move Canadarm2 to put Menon and the array at the ISS port-installation site, supporting the 2A electrical-power channel.

Each array is about 10 feet (3 meters) long when folded up and weighs 750 pounds (340 kilograms) here on Earth, according to Garrett Hehn, NASA's spacewalk flight director. The agency therefore knows the iROSAs are "a lot to handle," he said during a press conference on Oct. 20 that previewed the two upcoming spacewalks.

As such, NASA looked at how previous iROSA spacewalks were performed and created a new "elegant series of maneuvers, where we've tried to rotate around the actual center of mass of the arrays, rather than the crew member," Hehn added. "It was a lesson learned from previous EVAs, of how we thought we could make it a little less tiring on Anil."

Kutryk will move over to the installation location, hand-over-hand, to join Menon. There, the two will place the IROSA onto the older solar array, using a "mod kit" placed on a previous spacewalk. "We've got a series of bolts to structurally attach it [the IROSA] and release, in order for this folded-up configuration to fold open, and basically go from about 10 feet long to around 20 feet [6 m] long," Hehn explained.

"These arrays," he added, "I kind of think of them like a snap bracelet … They basically have a series of magnets up the side, where they deploy with enough energy that it just continues rolling out steadily. That process will take about 10 minutes on the day of the EVA."

Following that, the astronauts need to access power cables at a time when that area of the ISS is not in sunlight; the station will be (as always) moving through its orbit, circling the Earth every 90 minutes, so timing will be important.

"We can't have any sun on the arrays, whenever we're handling those hot cables," Hehn said. "Basically, we'll use a jumper to bring together both the legacy arrays' power, and this new rollout solar arrays' power, in order to have a pretty substantial gain to our power-generation capability."

The Nov. 5 EVA will essentially have the astronauts do the same installation procedure with another array, this time heading to the starboard side of the space station. The last IROSA installation, however, will take place a little farther from the station, beyond Canadarm2's reach. So the astronauts will do a "leapfrog" to get out there.

After Menon, the array and Canadarm2 are brought to the installation location, Hehn said, Kutryk — moving to the same location by himself, hand over hand — will go into another platform installed on the station truss, and take the IROSA from Menon's hands. As Kutryk waits in place, Menon will exit the robotics platform, move it from the Canadarm2 to another spot on the space station's truss, and then get back on to the platform to hold the IROSA securely for installation for the 3B electrical-power channel.

"This is the way that we close that final distance that the robotic arm is unable to do on its own," Hehn said.

Canadian robots, support teams — and new funding

The CSA's last spacewalk was during the agency's previous mission seven years ago, which involved astronaut David Saint-Jacques. On April 8, 2019, Saint-Jacques successfully fought difficult equipment during a busy excursion alongside NASA astronaut Anne McClain.

CSA has a 2.3% contribution to ISS, usually working out to a flight every five or six years. However, Kutryk's slot was delayed two years, from 2024 to 2026, because he was originally assigned to fly up on Boeing's Starliner capsule, which needs more flight testing following numerous issues that cropped up during its crewed demonstration flight in 2024.

Kutryk, who launched Oct. 1 aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon with three other astronauts, has generated a lot of political and industry excitement in Canada. His mission marks a rare pair of CSA astronaut launches in a single year, as Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen just launched in April. (The last time this happened was in 2009, when Robert Thirsk was doing a long-duration station excursion and Julie Payette visited during a two-week space shuttle mission.)

Canadian astronaut missions are unusual, even when including private missions — or non-CSA government astronauts, like now-retired NASA astronaut Andrew Feustel, who has dual U.S.-Canadian citizenship. Canada is therefore using the new CSA mission as a catalyst. In recent weeks, Canada announced several government and industry commitments to keep the momentum going even after Kutryk returns next spring.

For example, Canada just announced its first bipartisan space caucus, named Hansen a space advisor to the prime minister, pledged to soon give CSA its first space strategy since 2019, and promised, if at all possible, to announce a mission assignment for Gibbons within the next year. (The latter may depend on factors such as NASA's availability for missions, as Canada does not launch astronauts on its own.)

On the industry side, Canada's defense department last week promised the launch company NordSpace $20 million CDN ($14 million USD) for a 10-year launch pad access agreement at the company's young spaceport in the province Newfoundland and Labrador; additional mission costs will be paid when those are ordered. Canada also recently promised $200 million CDN ($140 million USD) to Maritime Launch Services over 10 years, committing to a launch pad at the company's emerging spaceport in Nova Scotia.

]]> <![CDATA[ Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane ]]> Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.

Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents.

The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.

Apeiron was one of four finalist names that Virgin Galactic narrowed down from a list of 276 employee-submitted suggestions. After the public weighed in, Apeiron came out on top over Horizon, Explorer and Ascend.

“Apeiron, the Boundless, captures the ambition of human spaceflight and the possibilities it opens for humanity," Virgin Galactic CEO Michael Golglazier said in a company statement. "The extraordinary response to the public vote made choosing this name even more meaningful."

The shiny new space plane will be attached to Virgin Galactic's VMS Eve carrier aircraft for its journey to Spaceport America, where engineers will complete work on its avionics software ahead of Apeiron's first flight tests and eventual operational missions.

The new Delta-class vehicle replaces Virgin's earlier space plane model, VSS Unity, which flew seven suborbital missions during its operational lifetime between the summers of 2023 and 2024. The company suspended VSS Unity flights to focus efforts on Apeiron's development, and now hopes to begin flying customers again in mid-2027.

Once they're in regular operation, Virgin plans to fly each of its Delta-class vehicles as many as eight times a month. A second Delta-class space plane is already under construction and is expected to join Apeiron at Spaceport America around the same time that Virgin restarts flying passengers, about 675 of whom are still waiting in line with tickets for a seat on one of the company's suborbital jaunts, according to the company's Q2 2026 SEC filing.

Now, more than 100 of those future space travelers are beginning their initial preparations for flight, with more ticketholders expected to follow once Virgin brings the second Delta-class vehicle into service. When the company began selling seats aboard its space plane in 2014, when VSS Unity was still under construction, tickets were priced around $200,000. Today, that price has jumped to $850,000 per seat, according to a report by Latte.

Like its predecessor, Apeiron and future Delta-class vehicles are designed for short, suborbital spaceflights, and are not capable of reaching orbit around Earth. They fly above the internationally recognized boundary of space, the 100-kilometer-high (62 miles) Karman line, and provide those onboard with several minutes of weightlessness and great views of the planet below.

Virgin Galactic plans to share further details about its upcoming flight tests during its November earnings call.

Virgin is one of two American companies that have flown paying customers to suborbital space and back. The other, Blue Origin, suspended its flights earlier this year to focus on helping land NASA astronauts on the moon.

A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit.

An iceberg has quickly escaped from the Weddell Sea in Antarctica, on its way to an icy new destination.

What is it?

As captured by a satellite in orbit, the Antarctic iceberg A-81 has quite quickly (for an iceberg) parted ways from its icy home, breaking off to drift toward a shallow underwater shelf in Georgia.

The 600-square-mile (1,550-square-kilometer) iceberg first broke off from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January of 2023. Now, generally speaking, giant icebergs don't travel that fast. But In just three years, this massive iceberg has traveled 1,400 miles (2,300 kilometers) north of the Brunt Ice Shelf. For an iceberg, that's really fast.

Over this time period, the iceberg drifted through the Weddell Sea in Antarctica's Southern Ocean before reaching the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, floating further into the Scotia Sea and then finally now reaching the edge of a remote island in South Georgia.

In this satellite snapshot captured on Oct. 20, 2026, we can see the iceberg in its current location near an underwater shelf off the coast of South Georgia. While it isn't abnormal for icebergs like A-81 to break off from larger ice shelves, Brunt has recently had multiple large icebergs break off one quickly after the other, according to a statement from NASA.

Why is it incredible?

This image was captured by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), an instrument on board NASA's Terra satellite.

Earth-observing satellites like Terra keep a close eye on changes on our home planet. In addition to this image, observations from Terra have showed how the iceberg has traveled over the last few years.

With satellites like Terra, scientists can keep a close eye on these changes in Antarctic ice, which is becoming increasingly important as climate change continues to progress across the globe, affecting everything from Arctic ice to sea levels rising, worsening natural disasters and more.

The powerful Vera Rubin Observatory has spotted what seems to be a dwarf planet circling the sun in the frigid depths beyond Neptune.

The icy object, known as 2026 ED138, is likely between 600 and 1500 kilometers (373 to 972 miles) wide, scientists say. It's therefore probably big enough to be sculpted into a sphere by its own gravity — a key characteristic that separates dwarf planets from asteroids and other small space rocks.

And if 2026 ED138 is indeed a dwarf planet, that's a pretty big deal, as astronomers have confirmed just five of them to date: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

2026 ED138 was discovered by Matthew Holman, who works at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian (CfA). The big moment came on Oct. 13, when Holman was running previously collected Rubin data through a search code that he developed with his CfA colleague Kevin Napier.

That search revealed a mysterious object beyond Neptune's orbit. Despite its immense distance from the sun, this body was relatively bright, suggesting that it's larger than the average trans-Neptunian object.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said in a statement on Tuesday (Oct. 27), the day the discovery of 2026 ED138 was announced. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

Those checks involved a thorough search through Rubin's catalog. And that catalog is pretty heft, even though Rubin is a pretty new scope.

The Vera Rubin Observatory sits atop Cerro Pachón, an 8,799-foot-tall (2,682 meters) mountain in northern Chile, and features a primary mirror 28 feet (8.4 m) wide. The scope achieved first light in April 2025 and began its main project, the 10-year-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), in June of this year.

During the LSST, Rubin images the entire southern sky every few days using a 3.2-gigapixel camera, the largest digital camera ever built for astronomy. This work creates a high-resolution time-lapse "movie" that can reveal a great deal about the cosmos.

For example, astronomers think Rubin will shed light on dark energy and dark matter, the mysterious stuff that together makes up most of the universe's mass-energy budget. Its observations will also serve as a solar system inventory, helping scientists map out our cosmic backyard like never before. Rubin has already discovered more than 11,000 new asteroids, for example, with many more surely to come.

The LSST inventory will likely include a number of new dwarf planets as well — including, possibly, 2026 ED138. For the object definitely exists: Holman and his colleague Mario Jurić, who works at the University of Washington and serves as Rubin Solar System Lead Scientist, found that Rubin spotted 2026 ED138 30 separate times on 20 nights between March 4 and July 11 of this year.

And further digging revealed that the Dark Energy Camera (DEC), an instrument on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile, also spotted 2026 ED138. Indeed, DEC observations of the object go all the way back to 2016.

The data show that 2026 ED138's orbit is tilted by about 25 degrees relative to the plane of the solar system. It therefore likely had a gravitational interaction with Neptune, which knocked it off kilter, scientists say.

2026 ED138 currently lies about 46 astronomical units (AU) from the sun. (One AU is the Earth-sun distance — about 93 million miles, or 150 million kilometers). This puts it beyond Pluto's average distance from the sun, which is roughly 40 AU.

There is still much to learn about the object, however. For example, we won't know whether or not it's a dwarf planet until astronomers nail down its size. And that will require observations in infrared light, the range of wavelengths that NASA's James Webb Space Telescope is optimized for.

So stay tuned: There's doubtless more news about 2026 ED138 coming, and Rubin could turn up more worlds like it in the coming months and years.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

Alongside that reveal, the company will also announce the spacecraft's name, selected through a public vote held across more than 80 countries.

Simultaneously, the company is also working on a second Delta-class vehicle, which it hopes to enter into service before the end of next year. And, with the first Delta vehicle leaving the nest, the company's Mesa factory is shifting focus to the completion of the second which will lead to structural testing and preparations for its rocket engine assembly.

Virgin Galactic announced its Delta manufacturing plans in 2022, initially anticipating research flights to begin in late 2025 and passenger service in 2026. Those plans have since run into multiple delays. The company said its revised schedule allows for the additional time needed to integrate and validate the spacecraft's avionics software, with final testing to take place at Spaceport America.

Its Delta vehicle will replace Virgin's earlier spaceplane model, VSS Unity, which began operations in June 2023, and completed seven commercial missions before its final flight on June 8, 2024. Virgin suspended Unity's commercial flights to concentrate on developing the next-generation fleet, which is designed to carry more passengers and fly considerably more frequently.

Each Delta-class vehicle is equipped to accommodate up to six passengers, compared with Unity's four, and is expected to complete as many as eight spaceflights per month — more than 10 times the rate Virgin was flying Unity.

When Virgin Galactic began selling seats aboard its planned spaceplane in 2004, tickets cost about $200,000 apiece. By 2014, nearly 700 people had reserved spots on future flights. Now, more than 100 of those future space travelers are beginning their initial preparations, with additional ticketholders expected to follow as the company works toward operating two spaceships by the second half of 2027.

Virgin Galactic plans to share live updates during Wednesday's transport flight, weather and technical conditions permitting, and provide further details about its upcoming flight tests during its November earnings call.

 <description>Bude naše dítě chodit do běžné školy? Bude moci sportovat, řídit auto nebo si vybrat jakékoliv povolání?  <description>Izrael stále čeká na konečné výsledky parlamentních voleb. Momentálně se čeká zejména na sečtení korespondenčních hlasů od vojáků nasazených v okupovaných územích.  <description>Americká výletní loď, která podniká cestu kolem světa a své kajuty propagovala jako plovoucí domovy, kde mohou pasažéři trvale žít, přerušila plavbu v Kambodži kvůli stoupajícím nákladům na palivo. Dvě stovky cestujících musely plavidlo opustit a zajistit si ubytování na pevnině. Tito lidé netušili, co s nimi bude dál, napsala ve čtvrtek agentura AP.</description>

 <description>Španělsko se ve čtvrtek ráno probudilo do státního smutku, který jeho vláda vyhlásila kvůli tragické srážce dvou vysokorychlostních vlaků.  <description>Strana Likud izraelského premiéra Benjamina Netanjahua obvinila strany izraelských Arabů, že ukradly parlamentní volby. Podle předběžných výsledků nezíská ve 120členném Knesetu většinu ani Netanjahuova koalice, ani opozice. Uskupení Jednotná kandidátka, které se do parlamentu také dostane a které sdružuje několik stran izraelských Arabů, je podle jeho šéfa připraveno podpořit vládu složenou z opozičních stran, do vlády samotné by ale nevstoupilo.</description>

 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/lide-se-snazili-dostat-ven-okny-vychody-zablokovaly-kufry-u-spanelskeho-toleda_2610281900_zko</link>
 <description>Nejméně 68 lidí zemřelo po srážce dvou vysokorychlostních vlaků poblíž španělského města Urda v provincii Toledo. Vlak státního dopravce Renfe AVE narazil do stojící soupravy soukromé společnosti Iryo. Celkem tři vagony se po nárazu zřítily z náspu. Jeden z poškozených vagonů byl po nárazu roztržen. Španělský ministr dopravy Puente Santiago dodatečně oznámil, že nehodu způsobilo chybné rozhodnutí centrálního dispečerského pracoviště.</description>

 <description>Ve Spojených státech zesiluje odpor proti výstavbě datových center, která jsou nezbytná pro rozvoj umělé inteligence. Jejich provoz vyžaduje značné množství elektřiny a vody, místní obyvatelé si navíc stěžují na hluk a další dopady na životní prostředí i lidské zdraví. Nakolik se výstavba datových center promítá do kampaně před listopadovými volbami do Kongresu? A proč ji navzdory odporu části vlastních příznivců podporuje Donald Trump?</description>

 <description>Počet obětí pondělního dronového útoku na tržiště v Súdánu vzrostl na 102. Dalších 113 lidí včetně žen a dětí utrpělo zranění. Zároveň zanikla místní buňka ANO v Turnově. Lídr turnovské kandidátky ANO Jaroslav Knížek (býv. ANO) to ČTK zdůvodnil tím, že nechtějí být zatíženi celostátní politikou.</description></item><item><title>Po deseti letech seminářů přináší Markétina dopravní výchova bezplatný e-learning</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903846-po-deseti-letech-seminaru-prinasi-marketina-dopravni-vychova-bezplatny-e-learning.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/903846-po-deseti-letech-seminaru-prinasi-marketina-dopravni-vychova-bezplatny-e-learning.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 09:54:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Doprava</category><description>Pedagogové mateřských, základních i středních škol se od 26. 10. 2026 mohou vzdělávat v dopravní výchově online. Markétin dopravní e-learning je zdarma, zabere přibližně čtyři až šest hodin a dá se procházet po částech, kdykoli a odkudkoli.</description></item><item><title>Úleva pro řidiče v Liberci. Od neděle projedou po opravené polovině mostu na průtahu I/35</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904305-ridici-od-nedele-projedou-po-opravene-polovine-mostu-na-prutahu-i-35-v.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/904305-ridici-od-nedele-projedou-po-opravene-polovine-mostu-na-prutahu-i-35-v.html</guid><pubDate>Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:32:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Řidiči od neděle 1. listopadu znovu projedou po opravené polovině mostu na průtahu I/35 v Liberci ve směru na Děčín. Práce na mostě nedaleko nákupní zóny Sever začaly v polovině června, od té doby je provoz převedený na druhou polovinu čtyřpruhu v režimu 1+1.</description></item><item><title>Chtěl ukrást maso, pak rozpoutal bitku: S ostrahou se rval přímo v obchodě</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904304-chtel-ukrast-maso-pak-rozpoutal-bitku-s-ostrahou-se-rval-primo-v-obchode.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/904304-chtel-ukrast-maso-pak-rozpoutal-bitku-s-ostrahou-se-rval-primo-v-obchode.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:20:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>V násilnický incident přerostl pokus o krádež tří kusů vepřového masa v obchodním domě Andy v České Lípě. Sedmadvacetiletý muž se po odhalení pokusil ostrahu fyzicky napadnout a agresivně se choval i po příjezdu městské policie. Nakonec skončil v rukou policie státní.</description></item><item><title>Boulder Point zdvojnásobil svou velikost. Lezení přitom není jen pro sportovce</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904150-boulder-point-zdvojnasobil-svou-velikost-lezeni-pritom-neni-jen-pro-sportovce.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/904150-boulder-point-zdvojnasobil-svou-velikost-lezeni-pritom-neni-jen-pro-sportovce.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:54:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Sport</category><description>Liberecké lezecké centrum Boulder Point vstoupilo do nové éry. Osm let od svého otevření rozšířilo své prostory a dnes nabízí 2 000 metrů čtverečních pro bouldering. Chce vytvářet místo, kam se lidé rádi vracejí nejen kvůli lezení.</description></item><item><title>Na průčelí baziliky v Jablonném v Podještědí se vrátila další kamenná socha</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/904298-na-pruceli-baziliky-v-jablonnem-v-podjestedi-se-navrati-dalsi-kamenna-socha.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/kultura/904298-na-pruceli-baziliky-v-jablonnem-v-podjestedi-se-navrati-dalsi-kamenna-socha.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 16:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Kultura</category><description>Na průčelí baziliky svatého Vavřince a svaté Zdislavy v Jablonném v Podještědí na Liberecku se v úterý  vrátila třetí z pěti soch. Opět jde o kopii původní pískovcové sochy, kterou před třemi staletími vytvořil barokní sochař Franz Bienert. Originály nelze kvůli špatnému stavu na balustrádu vrátit.</description></item><item><title>Světový den spoření slaví 102 let. Víte, jak jsou vaše úspory chráněné?</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903749-svetovy-den-sporeni-slavi-102-let-vite-jak-jsou-vase-uspory-chranene.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/903749-svetovy-den-sporeni-slavi-102-let-vite-jak-jsou-vase-uspory-chranene.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 13:54:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Společnost</category><description>Už 102 let si připomínáme na konci října Světový den spoření. Jeho původním cílem bylo povzbudit lidi k vytváření úspor a posílit důvěru ve finanční instituce. Dnes máme pro ukládání a zhodnocování peněz mnohem více možností než naši předkové.</description></item><item><title>Nádherný výhled po 70 letech. Na Javorníku slavnostně otevřeli novou rozhlednu</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904296-nadherny-vyhled-po-70-letech-na-javorniku-slavnostne-otevreli-novou-rozhlednu.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904296-nadherny-vyhled-po-70-letech-na-javorniku-slavnostne-otevreli-novou-rozhlednu.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 13:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Na Javorníku u Liberce se ve středu 28. října slavnostně otevřela nová rozhledna u hotelu Obří sud. Nabízí nejvýše položený vyhlídkový ochoz v kraji a výhled z výšky více než 34 metrů. Přestože oficiální zahájení proběhlo dnes, ve zkušebním provozu ji během předchozího měsíce navštívily tisíce lidí.</description></item><item><title>Vlastní zkušenost místo diplomu? Peer může pomoci i ublížit</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904207-vlastni-zkusenost-misto-diplomu-peer-muze-pomoci-i-ublizit.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904207-vlastni-zkusenost-misto-diplomu-peer-muze-pomoci-i-ublizit.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 11:08:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Markéta Hamerníková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Prošel si depresí, závislostí nebo poruchou příjmu potravy a teď pomáhá lidem, kteří jsou tam, kde byl kdysi on. Takzvaní peer konzultanti přinášejí do péče o duševní zdraví něco, co se nedá vystudovat – vlastní zkušenost. Právě ta ale může být zároveň rizikem.</description></item><item><title>Československo slaví 108 let od svého vzniku. Co se stalo 28. října?</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904205-ceskoslovensko-slavi-108-let-od-sveho-vzniku-co-se-stalo-28-rijna.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/904205-ceskoslovensko-slavi-108-let-od-sveho-vzniku-co-se-stalo-28-rijna.html</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 09:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Petr Roubíček</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>28. říjen – pro někoho jen další státní svátek, pro druhé chvíle, kdy je dobré připomenout si vznik samostatného Československého státu. Jednalo se o jeden z nástupnických států rozpadlého Rakousko-Uherska. Tehdejší Československo zahrnovalo území Čech, Moravy, Slezka, Slovenska a Podkarpatské Rusi.</description></item></channel></rss>
